title: How Lighthouse Keepers Ate, Washed & Slept on a Rock in the Sea
asof: History from National Records of Scotland & a UK pay report (c. 1971) · sources in description

shots.s: Three men live inside this tower.
It stands on a rock, eleven miles out to sea.
At high tide, the waves cover the rock completely.
Their bedroom is round.
There's no shower.
For a long time, there wasn't even a toilet.
So how did lighthouse keepers eat,
wash,
and sleep,
on a rock in the sea?
This is the Bell Rock Lighthouse,
off the east coast of Scotland.
It was finished in 1810.
It's the oldest working sea-washed lighthouse in the world.
The tower is built of stone, from the rock up.
Inside, rooms are stacked on top of each other,
like a tube of coins.
At the bottom, stores.
Then the kitchen.
Then the bedroom.
And at the top, the light.
Three keepers were on duty at a time.
Their main job: keep the light burning,
all night, every night.
A clockwork machine turned the lamp
and rang the fog bell.
It had to be wound up every thirty minutes.
So keepers split the night into watches of three or four hours.
Watches changed every night,
so nobody got the same watch twice in a row.
Between watches, you sleep in the bedroom.
It's a circle, about thirteen feet across.
Three bunks, curved to fit the wall.
A curtain for privacy.
And outside, the sea hammers the tower.
In the morning,
the keeper who had the last night watch made breakfast for everyone.
Food came out by boat.
But the sea decided when.
A UK government report in the early 1970s described rock station food:
meager and monotonous.
Sometimes supplies were ruined,
soaked by seawater on the way out.
Every day, the keepers measured the oil,
paraffin and water left.
Because nobody knew when the next boat could land.
Fresh water had to be rationed.
So for the whole stay on the rock,
there was no shower or bath.
And the toilet?
Bell Rock didn't get one until 1964.
A saltwater unit.
The report said sanitary conditions were sometimes primitive.
At first, keepers stayed on the rock for six weeks,
then two weeks ashore.
Later it became two months on, one month off.
By the 1970s, one month on,
one month off.
But in bad weather, the relief boat couldn't land.
So you waited.
Families lived ashore,
at the signal tower in Arbroath.
The two sides talked with flags
and a big copper ball.
It's said that when a keeper's baby was born,
they'd fly trousers for a boy,
or a dress for a girl.
Sometimes the sea won.
In December 1900, on the Flannan Isles,
far to the west,
a passing steamer noticed the light was out.
On the twenty-sixth,
a relief keeper named Joseph Moore landed.
The station was empty.
Lamps cleaned and ready. The kitchen tidy.
Two sets of outdoor gear were missing.
Three keepers were never found.
The inquiry found storm damage at the landing.
It concluded a huge wave probably swept them into the sea.
Over time, machines took over.
In 1998, the last lighthouse in Scotland was automated.
The keepers came ashore for good.
The lights still flash every night,
with nobody inside.
Could you live a month in a stone tube in the sea?
